'''Rachel M. Fewster''' (born 9 June 1974) is a British and New Zealand [[Environmental statistics|environmental statistician]] and statistical ecologist known for her work on wildlife population size, population genetics, and [[Benford's law]], and for the development of the CatchIT [[citizen science]] project for monitoring [[invasive species]].{{r|campbell|connect}} She is a professor of statistics in New Zealand at the [[University of Auckland]].{{r|directory}}

==Research==
A common theme of Fewster's research has been the study of [[invasive species]].{{r|campbell}} Her research on [[List of islands of New Zealand|New Zealand offshore islands]] has shown that rats can swim hundreds of metres from one island to another, and therefore that eradicating rats on the islands requires keeping all nearby islands rat-free as well.{{r|rat}}

==Education and career==
Fewster read mathematics at the [[University of Cambridge]] from 1992 to 1995, and earned a PhD in statistics at the [[University of St Andrews]] in 1999.{{r|cv}} On completing her doctorate, she was offered a position as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Auckland, and has remained there since then.{{r|campbell}} She has been a full professor since 2019.{{r|inaugural}}

==Recognition==
Fewster won a National Tertiary Teaching Excellence Award in 2009.{{r|teaching}} She is the 2018 winner of the Campbell Award of the New Zealand Statistical Association.{{r|campbell}}
